summary: Over roughly forty minutes, asset-A did four things that are unremarkable alone and hard to explain together: it reached forty ports on one internal neighbour, failed twelve authentications inside ninety seconds, then began contacting an external address every sixty seconds, and finally sent 400 MiB outbound — about eighty times its own weekly p95. The ordering is what makes this worth an analyst's time.

claims.text: asset-A reached 40 distinct ports on a single internal host inside ten minutes, with no reply on any of them.
Twelve authentication failures from asset-A fell inside a ninety-second window.
Fourteen connections to one external address, sixty seconds apart with jitter near 1.6%.
The hour's outbound volume was far above the seven-day baseline for this asset.
Regular fixed-interval callbacks with very low jitter are a widely documented command-and-control pattern.
Port scanning followed by credential attempts is a common early sequence in intrusion reporting.

recommendations.detail: Establish what asset-A was running during the window.
The owner may recognise the transfer as a scheduled job.
Confirm the seven-day baseline covers a representative week.
Look for the same interval on other assets.

limitations: This packet carries derived measurements only: no process, user or command-line context, and every address and name is an opaque token. It cannot tell you whether the transfer was authorised, and it is not evidence of compromise on its own.
